entry: Probability distribution of the sum of the squares of k independent standard [[Normal distribution|normal]] random variables, where k is the number of degrees of freedom. It is a special case of the [[Gamma distribution|gamma distribution]] and is used mainly in hypothesis testing, including the [[Chi-squared test|chi-squared test of independence]], and, when the underlying distribution is normal, in constructing [[Confidence interval|confidence intervals]] for population variance. It is also a component of the t- and F-distributions.

Statistical hypothesis test for comparing observed and expected frequencies in categorical data. Published by [[Karl Pearson|Karl Pearson]] in 1900, Pearson's chi-squared test is considered one of the foundations of modern statistics. It determines whether there is a statistically significant difference between expected and observed frequencies in one or more categories of a contingency table, and it can test whether two categorical variables are independent. The test statistic, the sum of (observed − expected)² / expected across categories, approximately follows a [[Chi-squared distribution|chi-squared distribution]] when samples are large. Fisher's exact test is used instead for contingency tables with small samples. Its [[P-value|p-value]] is used to reject or retain the null hypothesis of no association.

Chinese military commander and statesman, head of the Nationalist government from 1925 to 1948 and president of the Republic of China from 1948 to 1975. As commandant of the Whampoa Military Academy from 1924, he led the Northern Expedition (1926–1928), which largely unified China under a Nationalist government based in Nanjing. His purge of [[Chinese Communist Party|Chinese Communist Party]] members in the Shanghai massacre triggered the [[Chinese Civil War|Chinese Civil War]]. He later led China in the [[Second Sino-Japanese War|Second Sino-Japanese War]] (1937–1945), mostly from [[Chongqing|Chongqing]]. In 1949 his [[Kuomintang|Kuomintang]] was defeated by [[Mao Zedong|Mao Zedong's]] forces, and he retreated to [[Taiwan|Taiwan]], where he imposed martial law. Supporters credit him with unifying China and resisting Japan, while critics fault his early appeasement of Japan, the deliberate flooding of the Yellow River and authoritarian rule on the mainland and Taiwan.

City in northern [[Thailand|Thailand]], administrative center of its namesake province (urban pop., 2023: about 1.2 million). Founded in 1296 as the new capital of the Lan Na kingdom, succeeding Chiang Rai, it lies about 700 km north of [[Bangkok|Bangkok]] in the Thai highlands. The old city is enclosed by a moat and remnants of ancient red brick walls. It was occupied by the Toungoo Empire in 1556, and in 1774 it became part of the Thonburi Kingdom. In 2006 the city hosted the Chiang Mai Initiative between [[ASEAN|ASEAN]] and China, Japan and South Korea. In 2017 the [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] Creative Cities Network named it a City of Crafts and Folk Arts. Tourism is a major part of its economy.

Most populous city in the U.S. state of [[Illinois|Illinois]], on the western shore of [[Lake Michigan|Lake Michigan]] (pop., 2020: 2.74 million). Incorporated in 1837 near a portage between the [[Great Lakes|Great Lakes]] and [[Mississippi River|Mississippi River]] watersheds, it grew rapidly in the mid-19th century. The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed several square miles and left more than 100,000 people homeless. The city contributed to [[Urban planning|urban planning]] and architecture through the Chicago School, the City Beautiful movement and the steel-framed [[Skyscraper|skyscraper]], and the [[Willis Tower|Willis Tower]] is among the tallest buildings in the Western Hemisphere. Its derivatives market is the largest and most diverse in the world, generating 20% of all commodities and financial futures volume. The city's transit system is the second-largest in the U.S., and its culture has made major contributions to jazz, blues, soul, hip-hop and house music. The [[University of Chicago|University of Chicago]] is among its institutions of higher education.

Professional basketball team in the [[National Basketball Association|National Basketball Association]] (NBA), based in Chicago, Illinois. Founded in 1966, the Bulls won six NBA championships between 1991 and 1998, led by [[Michael Jordan|Michael Jordan]], Scottie Pippen and coach Phil Jackson. Their 72 wins in the 1995–96 season set an NBA record that stood until the Golden State Warriors won 73 games in 2015–16. The team has struggled to regain its former success since 1998.

[[American Mafia|Italian American Mafia]] crime family based in Chicago, Illinois. It rose to power in the 1920s under Johnny Torrio and [[Al Capone|Al Capone]], during gang wars over illegal alcohol in Prohibition. After Capone's 1931 conviction for income tax evasion, it was run by Paul Ricca and Tony Accardo. The Outfit has been involved in loansharking, illegal gambling, prostitution, extortion and murder. It is considered one of the most violent Mafia families in the United States, with over 1,000 murders since the 1920s, and its influence has declined since the late 20th century.

American rock band formed in [[Illinois|Illinois]] in 1967. Its songs often combine rock with elements of [[Classical music|classical music]], [[Jazz|jazz]], R&B and pop, and the band is known for its horn section. Robert Lamm, Lee Loughnane and James Pankow have remained constant members, although the lineup has been fluid since 2009. The band has sold more than 100 million records, and in 1971 it became the first rock act to sell out Carnegie Hall for a week. It was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2016.

Large pre-Columbian city built by the Maya people in Yucatán state, [[Mexico|Mexico]]. The Maya name means "At the mouth of the well of the Itzá", the Itzá being an [[Lineage (anthropology)|ethnic-lineage group]] that dominated the northern peninsula. The city was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands from the Late Classic period (c. 600–900 AD) into the early Postclassic (c. 900–1200 AD). Its architecture combines Maya styles with styles from central Mexico, which most contemporary interpretations see as the result of cultural diffusion rather than conquest. Four natural sinkholes, called [[Cenote|cenotes]], provided water in the [[Karst|karst]] landscape. It is one of the most visited archaeological sites in Mexico, with over 2.6 million tourists in 2017, and the state of Yucatán bought the land around the monuments in 2010.

Meat of the domesticated [[Chicken|chicken]] (*Gallus gallus domesticus*), the most common type of [[Poultry|poultry]] and the second most consumed meat in the world, after [[Pork|pork]]. Chicken is prepared by baking, grilling, barbecuing, frying, boiling and roasting, and it has been a staple of [[Fast food|fast food]] since the latter half of the 20th century. Modern chickens descend from red junglefowl hybrids and grey junglefowl first raised thousands of years ago in the northern [[Indian subcontinent|Indian subcontinent]]. Chicken was one of the most common meats in the [[Middle Ages|Middle Ages]]. In the United States, consumption rose during World War II because of beef and pork shortages. Chicken meat was the most produced type of meat in 2021, just ahead of pig meat. It is sometimes cited as healthier than red meat, with lower cholesterol and saturated fat.

Indo-British [[Curry|curry]] of roasted, marinated chicken pieces in a creamy spiced sauce. It is thought to have been created in Britain, possibly by Ali Ahmed Aslam in [[Glasgow|Glasgow]], although that account is disputed. It is one of the most popular dishes in Britain, and in 2001 the British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook called it "a true British national dish". The dish has been called inauthentic by both white Britons and South Asians. Scholars have debated its status, and some see it as a symbol of Britain's multicultural society.

Highly contagious, vaccine-preventable disease caused by the varicella-zoster virus, a member of the herpesvirus family. Also known as varicella, it produces an itchy rash of small blisters that scab over, usually beginning on the chest, back and face. Fever, tiredness and headache usually last five to seven days, and the disease is generally more severe in adults than in children. It spreads through airborne droplets and contact with blisters, and people are contagious from one or two days before the rash until all lesions have crusted over. Complications may include [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]], inflammation of the brain and bacterial skin infections. Since a varicella vaccine was introduced in the [[United States|United States]] in 1995, cases and complications have declined; the vaccine protects about 70–90 percent of people from disease. In 2015 chickenpox caused 6,400 deaths globally, down from 8,900 in 1990. Its connection to [[Shingles|shingles]] was determined in 1888.

Annual [[Legume|legume]] of the family [[Fabaceae|Fabaceae]], cultivated for its edible seeds (*Cicer arietinum*). It is known variously as gram, chana, garbanzo or Egyptian pea, and its seeds are high in protein. Chickpeas are a key ingredient in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines, where they are used in [[Hummus|hummus]] and [[Falafel|falafel]]. In Indian cuisine they feature in salads, soups, stews and curries, and India accounted for 75% of global chickpea production in 2023. Chickpeas are among the earliest cultivated legumes, and the oldest archaeological evidence of them was found in Syria. They were domesticated about 10,000 years ago alongside [[Wheat|wheat]], [[Barley|barley]], peas and [[Lentil|lentils]]. [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] described the species in *Species Plantarum* in 1753.

Perennial herbaceous plant of the family [[Asteraceae|Asteraceae]], usually with bright blue flowers (*Cichorium intybus*). Native to Europe, North Africa and western Asia, it has been introduced to the Americas, Australia and South Africa. It can grow to 1.5 m tall and flowers from March until October. Many varieties are cultivated for salad leaves, chicons or blanched buds, and the roots are baked, ground and used as a coffee substitute. Inulin, an extract from the root, is used in food manufacturing as a sweetener and source of dietary fiber. Chicory is grown as forage for [[Livestock|livestock]] and is also a [[Weed|weed]] of roadsides and disturbed land. Raw leaves are rich in vitamin K, vitamin A and vitamin C.

Prehistoric impact crater buried beneath the [[Yucatán Peninsula|Yucatán Peninsula]] in Mexico. It formed slightly over 66 million years ago, when an asteroid about 10 kilometers in diameter struck Earth. The crater is about 200 kilometers across and is buried about one kilometer beneath younger sedimentary rock. The impact coincides with the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary|Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary]] and is widely accepted as the main cause of the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]], which killed about 75% of plant and animal species, including all non-avian dinosaurs.

Top-ranking officer charged with managing a [[Company|company]] or [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit organization]]. CEOs report to the board of directors and are ultimately accountable for business decisions in areas such as operations, marketing and finance. The term was attested as early as 1782, when an ordinance of the Congress of the Confederation used it for the governors of the [[Thirteen Colonies|Thirteen Colonies]]. Subordinate executives usually include the chief operating officer and chief financial officer.

Chinese-American experimental physicist known for work in nuclear and particle physics. Born in Jiangsu province, China, she initially studied mathematics at National Central University in Nanjing before switching to physics. During the [[Manhattan Project|Manhattan Project]] she helped develop the gaseous diffusion process for separating uranium into [[Uranium-235|uranium-235]] and uranium-238 isotopes. Her best-known achievement was the Wu experiment, which proved that parity is not conserved in [[Weak interaction|weak interactions]]. The discovery led to her colleagues Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang winning the 1957 Nobel Prize in Physics, while Wu was awarded the inaugural Wolf Prize in Physics in 1978. Her nicknames included the "First Lady of Physics" and the "Queen of Nuclear Research".

Mexican breed of toy dog, the smallest recognized dog breed in the world. It is kept primarily as a [[Pet|companion animal]] and is characterized by its compact size, large erect ears and rounded skull, in short- and long-coated varieties. Genetic studies find a small proportion of pre-Columbian American dog ancestry. A 2020 study estimated it at about 4% in the Chihuahua, while an earlier 2013 study had suggested it might be as high as 70%. The American Kennel Club first registered a Chihuahua in 1904.

Desert ecoregion of northern [[Mexico|Mexico]] and the southwestern [[United States|United States]]. It occupies much of far West [[Texas|Texas]], the [[Rio Grande|Rio Grande]] and lower Pecos valleys of [[New Mexico|New Mexico]], part of southeastern Arizona, and the central and northern Mexican Plateau. With an area of about 501,896 sq km (193,783 sq mi), it is the largest hot desert in North America. Its largest continuous expanse lies in Mexico, mostly in the state of Chihuahua. The desert is fairly young, existing for only 8,000 years. It is mainly a rain-shadow desert, and most rain falls during the North American Monsoon between late June and early October. The World Wide Fund for Nature has described it as possibly the most biologically diverse desert in the world, although overgrazing has badly degraded much of it.

Work that interferes with children's schooling or is mentally, physically, socially or morally harmful. It is prohibited by legislation worldwide, though exceptions include child artists, family duties and supervised training. In the 19th and early 20th centuries many children aged 5–14 from poorer families worked in Western nations and their colonies, mainly in [[Agriculture|agriculture]], factories and [[Mining|mining]]. Industrial cities such as [[Manchester|Manchester]], [[Liverpool|Liverpool]] and [[Birmingham|Birmingham]] grew rapidly in Britain, and in the Victorian era children as young as four worked in factories and mines. Globally, the incidence of child labor fell from 25% to 10% between 1960 and 2003, according to the World Bank. In 2024 an estimated 138 million children were in child labor, including about 54 million in hazardous work, according to the ILO and [[UNICEF|UNICEF]]. Poverty and lack of schools are considered the primary causes, and agriculture is the largest employer of child labor.

Erotic material depicting persons under the local age of majority or [[Age of consent|age of consent]], also called child sexual abuse material (CSAM). Its legal definition varies by jurisdiction, but it is illegal in most. It is often produced through online solicitation, coercion and covert photography. Many laws also cover computer-generated images that appear to involve minors. In 2008, 94 [[Interpol|Interpol]] member states had laws specifically addressing child pornography. Since the 2000s, scholars and law enforcement have increasingly used terms such as "child abuse images", because "pornography" can carry an inaccurate implication of consent.

Form of child abuse in which a child is involved in sexual activity that they are not developmentally prepared for, cannot fully comprehend or cannot consent to. Child marriage is one of its main forms. Globally, nearly 1 in 8 girls experience sexual abuse before age 18. Most offenders know their victims: about 30% are relatives of the child, about 60% are other acquaintances and about 10% are strangers. Effects can include [[Depression (mood)|depression]], [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|post-traumatic stress disorder]], [[Anxiety|anxiety]] and [[Complex post-traumatic stress disorder|complex post-traumatic stress disorder]].

Completion of pregnancy, in which a fetus leaves the mother's body vaginally or by [[Caesarean section|cesarean section]] and becomes a newborn. Also called labor or delivery, it involved about 132 million human births globally in 2023. In developed countries most births occur in [[Hospital|hospitals]], while in developing countries most are home births. Vaginal birth is the most common mode and has three stages: opening of the [[Cervix|cervix]], delivery of the baby and delivery of the [[Placenta|placenta]]. Major health organizations advise placing the infant on the mother's chest immediately after birth, for skin-to-skin contact. Complications of pregnancy and childbirth cause about 260,000 birthing deaths each year, and seven million women have serious long-term problems.

Stories, books, magazines and poems created for children, classified by the intended age of the reader. Children's literature can be traced to fairy tales and songs from the oral tradition, though fairy tales were identified as children's literature only from the 17th century. From the 15th century, much literature was aimed at children, often with a moral or religious message. The concept of childhood in the 18th century led to a separate genre, starting with educational books, conduct books and simple ABCs. The late 19th and early 20th centuries are known as the Golden Age of Children's Literature, when [[Lewis Carroll|Lewis Carroll]]'s [[Alice's Adventures in Wonderland|Alice's Adventures in Wonderland]] appeared. The [[Harry Potter|Harry Potter]] series, written for children, is also popular with adults, leading [[The New York Times|The New York Times]] to create a separate bestseller list for children's books.

Country in the [[Southern Cone|Southern Cone]] of South America, the southernmost country in the world (pop., 2024: 18.5 million). Chile extends along a narrow strip between the [[Andes|Andes]] and the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]], bordering Peru, Bolivia and Argentina, with its capital at [[Santiago|Santiago]]. Spain conquered the region in the mid-16th century, and Chile declared independence in 1818. It gained its northern territory in the [[War of the Pacific|War of the Pacific]] (1879–83). In 1973 a coup, with support from the United States, overthrew the elected government of [[Salvador Allende|Salvador Allende]]. The military dictatorship that followed, led by [[Augusto Pinochet|Augusto Pinochet]], lasted until 1990 and was marked by widespread human rights violations, including more than 3,000 deaths and disappearances. Chile is a high-income economy and joined the [[OECD|OECD]] in 2010.
